title: How to Use Study Halls and Free Periods in IB DP2
summary: Learn how to use study halls and free periods during the IB DP2 fall term to finish coursework, revise actively, and reduce work after school.
body_markdown:
To **use study halls and free periods** efficiently during the IB DP2 fall term, decide on one specific outcome before each period. Match short periods to retrieval, planning, or administrative tasks, and reserve longer blocks for exam questions or defined coursework milestones.


This matters especially from September to November, when tests, coursework, the Extended Essay, TOK, CAS, and university applications may overlap. The aim is consistent progress while preserving energy for lessons and after-school work.


### Why the IB DP2 fall term feels crowded


This period is difficult because you may be learning new content while revising DP1 topics, preparing for tests, and responding to coursework feedback.


The IB uses both **internal and external assessment** , but schools determine many internal calendars and interim deadlines. There is no universal September deadline for every IA, EE, or TOK component, so your coordinator's calendar is the source of truth. The[IB overview of Diploma Programme assessment](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/assessment-and-exams/) explains the distinction between examinations, internally assessed work, and externally assessed coursework.


Five productive 35-minute periods create almost three additional hours of focused work each week. Their value comes from consistency rather than one unusually long session.


### Build one system for choosing tasks


Do not begin by opening several platforms and deciding what feels urgent. Maintain one master list of deadlines, coursework milestones, tests, applications, and personal commitments.


A practical priority order is:


1. **Urgent assessed work** , such as a submission due within several days.
2. **Blocked work** , where one action will allow later progress, such as asking about unclear feedback.
3. **High-value revision** , especially weak topics appearing in an approaching assessment.
4. **Maintenance tasks** , including flashcards, citations, file organization, and CAS records.


Use the[RevisionDojo IB Study Planner](https://www.revisiondojo.com/features/study-planner) or another calendar to assign tasks to periods. Schedule an outcome, such as “complete two integration questions and mark them,” rather than “study maths.”


### Match the task to the available period


A noisy 20-minute gap should not be treated like a quiet 60-minute study hall. Match the task to your available time and concentration.


Available time Suitable tasks Avoid


**10-15 minutes** Flashcards, citations, teacher email, paragraph planning, CAS reflection Starting a complex IA section


**20-30 minutes** Retrieval practice, short responses, source annotation, error-log review Attempting a full timed paper


**35-50 minutes** Exam questions, one coursework subsection, focused reading, essay planning Repeatedly switching subjects


**60 minutes or more** Timed paper section, substantial analysis, calculations, structured redrafting Using the entire block for organization


Use your clearest period for demanding reasoning and a low-energy period for routine work. Do not spend your best attention on formatting or inbox management.


### Follow a repeatable study hall routine


A productive period needs a defined beginning, working phase, and ending. For a 40-minute block, use this structure:


- **2 minutes:** Write the exact deliverable and open only the necessary materials.
- **25-30 minutes:** Work without messages, unrelated tabs, or subject switching.
- **5-8 minutes:** Check the work against a markscheme, rubric, or checklist.
- **2 minutes:** Record the next action for the following session.


For revision, use **retrieve, check, correct, schedule** . Attempt a question without help, compare it with reliable feedback, identify why marks were lost, and schedule a reattempt. The[RevisionDojo active recall guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/active-recall-for-ib-practice-questions) explains why producing an answer reveals more than rereading notes.


The[RevisionDojo Questionbank guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-question-bank-or-how-to-use-it-effectively) can help you create short, topic-specific practice sets. Consult Study Notes briefly when necessary, then return to the problem.


### Separate coursework from revision


Coursework and examination revision require different thinking. Label the period before beginning so one type of work does not drift into the other.


For coursework, choose a concrete milestone:


- label one graph and explain its significance
- evaluate one source
- draft one analytical paragraph
- check five citations against the bibliography
- revise one section using permitted teacher feedback
- prepare questions for a supervisor or subject teacher


The Extended Essay is an independent research project culminating in a **4,000-word paper** , according to the[official IB Extended Essay overview](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/extended-essay/) . Divide it into research, outlining, drafting, analysis, referencing, and checking rather than scheduling “work on EE.”


Keep submitted work authentically yours. The[IB academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) addresses behaviour that may create an unfair advantage. Jojo AI can explain concepts or question your reasoning, but it should not produce work submitted as your own.


### Adjust your plan from September to November


### September: establish control


Collect confirmed deadlines and convert large projects into milestones. Diagnose weak DP1 topics through short question sets. This prevents hidden work from becoming an October emergency.


### October: prioritize production


Use longer periods for coursework, analysis, and timed practice. Retain at least two brief retrieval sessions each week so coursework does not eliminate exam preparation. The[RevisionDojo time-management guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/time-management-in-ib-9-proven-tools-and-techniques-that-actually-work) explains how calendars, time blocks, and weekly reviews work together.


### November: close loops


Finish corrections, resolve missing citations, revisit repeated errors, and prepare for school assessments or mocks where applicable. Follow your school's calendar and move toward mixed, timed questions.


### Protect the conditions for focused work


Prepare before school by downloading documents and carrying required calculator equipment. Keep an offline task available in case the internet fails, and sit away from distractions when concentration matters.


If you have several free periods in one day, keep at least one for lunch, movement, or recovery. Working through every break can shift fatigue into lessons and evening study.


When a period ends, save the file clearly and write the next action. This prevents the next session from beginning with several minutes spent reconstructing your place.


### Common mistakes to avoid


- **Choosing by mood:** Easy or enjoyable subjects receive attention while urgent weaknesses remain.
- **Using vague labels:** “Do chemistry” provides no completion point.
- **Rewriting notes:** Attractive summaries may not test retrieval or application.
- **Starting full papers in short periods:** Fragmentation removes timing and stamina practice.
- **Ignoring feedback:** Practice without error analysis allows weaknesses to continue.
- **Working through every break:** Fatigue reduces the quality of later work.
- **Losing source records:** Missing citations create extra work and integrity concerns.


### A practical weekly template


Period Primary outcome


Monday Diagnose one weak topic with a short question set


Tuesday Complete one IA, EE, or TOK milestone


Wednesday Reattempt Monday's errors and review flashcards


Thursday Complete a timed question set or essay plan


Friday Close unfinished tasks and plan the next week


When a deadline approaches, assign an additional period to it without abandoning every other subject. The[RevisionDojo balanced study schedule](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-create-a-balanced-ib-study-schedule) offers guidance on distributing subject practice, core work, and recovery.


### Conclusion


To use study halls and free periods well, decide the outcome in advance, match it to the available time, focus on one task, and record the next step. Short periods suit recall and administration, while longer blocks suit exam practice and coursework milestones.
